subject: physics
title: Wave Equation and Wave Types
welcome_lead: Travel along a wave with v = f lambda and distinguish transverse from longitudinal motion.
meta_desc: A-Level Waves adventure on wave equation and classification of wave types.
final_note: Every wave obeys v = f lambda — from radio to gamma to sound.

concepts.def: Distance between two adjacent identical points.

v = f lambda; how fast the wave moves.

walkthroughs.body_html: v = f lambda relates speed (m/s), frequency (Hz) and wavelength (m). If frequency doubles at fixed speed, wavelength halves.
Oscillation is at right angles to direction of travel. These can be polarised. Examples: all electromagnetic waves and waves on strings.
Particles vibrate along the propagation direction creating compressions and rarefactions. They cannot be polarised. Example: sound in air.

options: Transverse

Electromagnetic
Polarised

mcqs.q: Doubling the frequency of a wave at fixed speed will:
options: Double wavelength
Halve wavelength
Quadruple wavelength
Leave wavelength unchanged

mcqs.q: When a wave travels through water, what happens to the water itself?
options: The water moves along with the wave from one place to another.
Electrons are sometimes waves and sometimes particles depending on the temperature of the apparatus.
The water oscillates about a fixed point; the wave transfers energy, not matter.
The water turns into wave material and changes state.

mcqs.q: Why does light bend when it enters a denser medium like glass?
options: Because gravity in the glass pulls the light down.
Because it slows down — the change in speed at the boundary causes the wavefront to bend (towards the normal).
The water turns into wave material and changes state.
Because the medium is denser, it physically blocks part of the light and forces it to turn.

mcqs.q: When does an electron behave as a wave?
options: Because gravity in the glass pulls the light down.
Electrons are sometimes waves and sometimes particles depending on the temperature of the apparatus.
Electrons are always waves and only look like particles at low energy.
In experiments that probe wave properties (e.g. diffraction through a crystal); in particle-like experiments it behaves as a particle.
